title: What Is Acetaldehyde? Alcohol's Toxic By-Product Explained
excerpt: Acetaldehyde is the toxic chemical your body makes when it breaks down alcohol. What it is, how it causes flushing and hangover symptoms, its cancer link, and how to limit it.
metaDescription: What is acetaldehyde? The toxic chemical your body makes from alcohol: how it causes flushing and hangovers, its cancer link, and how to limit it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** acetaldehyde is the chemical your body makes when it starts breaking down alcohol. It sits between the alcohol you drink and the harmless acetate your body ends up with, and it's far more toxic than alcohol itself. In most people it only exists for a short time, because a liver enzyme called ALDH2 clears it quickly. When that clean-up is slow, because of genetics, certain medicines, or simply drinking faster than your liver can keep up, acetaldehyde builds up and causes flushing, a racing heart, nausea, and headache. It's also the main reason health agencies classify alcohol as a cause of cancer.

**The quick facts:** Acetaldehyde (also called ethanal, chemical formula CH3CHO) is a small, reactive molecule. Your liver makes it from alcohol using an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), then turns it into acetate using aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH, mainly ALDH2). It likely contributes to hangovers, but researchers no longer think it's the whole story. It's also found in tobacco smoke, some foods and drinks, and industrial products. The reliable ways to limit your exposure are to drink less, drink slower, and not smoke while drinking.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on how the body processes alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** you get strong flushing, a pounding heart, hives, or nausea after only one or two drinks, especially if it's new. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you have trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, chest pain, fainting, or confusion after drinking, or if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is vomiting while drowsy, or is breathing slowly or irregularly. If you take disulfiram (Antabuse) or a medicine that warns against alcohol and you react after drinking, treat it as a medical problem, not a hangover.

## What Is Acetaldehyde? A Plain-English Definition

Acetaldehyde is an organic compound in the aldehyde family, the same chemical family as formaldehyde. It's a colorless liquid with a sharp, fruity smell that turns into a gas at about room temperature. Chemists also call it ethanal, and its formula is CH3CHO: two carbon atoms, four hydrogens, and one oxygen.

What makes acetaldehyde matter to anyone who drinks is where it comes from. When alcohol (ethanol) enters your body, it isn't removed in one step. Your liver first converts it into acetaldehyde, then converts the acetaldehyde into acetate, a mild compound similar to the acid in vinegar. The acetate is eventually broken down into carbon dioxide and water, or used for energy.

So acetaldehyde is the middle step, and it's the dangerous one. Alcohol is the drink, acetate is the harmless end product, and acetaldehyde is the toxic stop in between. Your body has evolved to move through that stop quickly, and most of the time it does.

### Why it's so reactive

Aldehydes have a chemical group that readily sticks to other molecules, including proteins and DNA. When acetaldehyde binds to these, it forms what scientists call "adducts," which are a bit like chemical scars. Adducts can stop proteins from working properly and can damage DNA in ways that lead to mutations. That reactivity is why even short bursts of high acetaldehyde cause noticeable symptoms, and why long-term exposure is linked to cancer.

## How Your Body Turns Alcohol Into Acetaldehyde (and Then Gets Rid of It)

Alcohol metabolism happens mostly in the liver, in two main steps. (For the full journey from first sip to exhale, see [how alcohol is metabolized](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized).)

1. **Alcohol to acetaldehyde.** The enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) does most of this work. Two backup systems pitch in too: an enzyme called CYP2E1 (which becomes more active in people who drink heavily on a regular basis) and an enzyme called catalase. Small amounts of ADH also work in the stomach lining.
2. **Acetaldehyde to acetate.** The enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) handles this step. The most important version is ALDH2, which works inside the mitochondria, the energy-producing parts of your cells. ALDH2 is very efficient, which is why acetaldehyde in the blood of most drinkers stays at low levels compared with alcohol.

A useful way to picture it is a two-stage factory line. Stage one (ADH) turns raw material into a hazardous intermediate. Stage two (ALDH2) turns the hazardous intermediate into something safe. As long as stage two keeps pace with stage one, the hazardous stuff never piles up. Problems start when stage one runs faster than stage two.

### What makes acetaldehyde build up

- **Drinking quickly.** Your liver can only process roughly one standard drink an hour, and that rate doesn't change much no matter what you do. Drinking faster pushes more alcohol into stage one at once. Our guide to [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains the timing in more detail.
- **A slow ALDH2 enzyme.** Some people inherit a version of ALDH2 that barely works. This is the cause of the classic "Asian flush," covered below.
- **A fast ADH enzyme.** Some people inherit a faster version of ADH (a variant of the ADH1B gene), so they produce acetaldehyde more quickly. This variant is more common in East Asian populations, and it can add to the effect of a slow ALDH2.
- **Medicines that block ALDH.** Disulfiram (Antabuse) works on purpose by blocking ALDH, so even a small amount of alcohol causes a sharp, unpleasant acetaldehyde reaction. Some other medicines carry warnings about similar reactions (more on that below).

## What Acetaldehyde Does to Your Body: The Symptoms

When acetaldehyde levels rise, the effects show up fast. People who flush describe them within minutes of starting to drink. The common ones are:

- **Facial flushing.** Acetaldehyde widens small blood vessels and is linked to the release of histamine, the same chemical involved in allergic reactions. The result is red, warm skin on the face, neck, and chest. Our guide to [Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) covers this in depth.
- **A racing or pounding heart.** As blood vessels widen and blood pressure dips, the heart speeds up to compensate.
- **Nausea and sometimes vomiting.** Acetaldehyde irritates the stomach and acts on the brain's nausea centers.
- **Headache.** Widened blood vessels and histamine are both thought to play a part.
- **Itching, hives, or a stuffy nose.** These are also histamine-type effects.
- **Feeling hot, dizzy, or unwell overall.** Some people describe it as a sudden feeling of being poisoned, which in a mild sense is exactly what's happening.

This set of symptoms has a name in medicine: the "alcohol flush reaction." It's the same thing disulfiram is designed to cause, just usually milder.

## Does Acetaldehyde Cause Hangovers?

This is the question most people are really asking, and the honest answer is: partly, probably, but not entirely.

For decades, acetaldehyde was the leading explanation for hangovers. It's toxic, it causes nausea and headache, and its symptoms look a lot like a bad morning after. It still plays some role. But researchers who study hangovers have pointed out a problem with the theory: hangovers tend to be worst when blood alcohol has dropped to around zero, and by then acetaldehyde levels in most people are also very low. If acetaldehyde were the main cause, you'd expect the worst symptoms while it was at its peak, not hours later.

Hangover researchers now think several things combine to cause a hangover:

- **Your immune system's response.** Studies have found raised levels of inflammatory signaling molecules (cytokines) during hangovers. That inflammation can produce the achy, foggy, flu-like feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but disrupts the second half of the night. Waking up tired makes everything feel worse.
- **Dehydration and stomach irritation.** These add to headache, thirst, and nausea, though dehydration alone doesn't explain hangovers.
- **Congeners.** These are other compounds in drinks, especially darker ones like bourbon, brandy, and red wine, that can make hangovers worse. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains them.
- **Acetaldehyde.** It likely contributes, especially in people who clear it slowly or who drink a lot quickly, and it may play a part in the inflammation and oxidative stress (a type of cell wear and tear caused by reactive molecules) that follow drinking.

The practical takeaway: lowering acetaldehyde exposure by drinking less and slower is sensible, but no product that only targets acetaldehyde should be expected to stop a hangover by itself. If you seem to get hangovers more easily than your friends, our article on [why some people get hangovers so easily](/never-hungover/why-do-i-get-hangovers-so-easily) walks through the other factors that matter.

## Acetaldehyde and Asian Flush: The ALDH2 Connection

The best-understood example of acetaldehyde build-up is the alcohol flush reaction often called "Asian flush" or "Asian glow."

It comes from a common variant of the ALDH2 gene (often written as ALDH2*2). People who carry one copy make an ALDH2 enzyme that works at a small fraction of normal speed. People with two copies have almost no working ALDH2 and usually feel so sick after even a small drink that they avoid alcohol altogether. The variant is common among people of East Asian descent, including Chinese, Japanese, and Korean populations. A widely cited 2009 review in PLoS Medicine by Brooks and colleagues estimated that more than a third of East Asians show the flushing response.

Because their stage-two enzyme is slow, people with this variant reach much higher acetaldehyde levels from the same amount of alcohol. That's why they turn red after one beer while friends without the variant don't.

### Why flushing isn't just cosmetic

The same 2009 review raised a serious point: people with the ALDH2 variant who drink regularly anyway appear to have a much higher risk of esophageal cancer than people with normal ALDH2 who drink the same amount. The likely reason is their tissues are exposed to more acetaldehyde for longer.

The authors also warned about a common workaround. Some people take antihistamine-type heartburn pills, such as famotidine (Pepcid), before drinking to hide the redness. These can reduce the visible flush, but they do nothing to lower acetaldehyde. Hiding the warning sign while the exposure continues can make people drink more than they otherwise would. If you flush, the redness is useful information, not just an embarrassment to cover up.
## Acetaldehyde and Cancer: What the Evidence Says

This is the part of the acetaldehyde story with the strongest scientific backing.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organization, classifies alcoholic drinks as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning there's enough evidence that they cause cancer in humans. In 2009, IARC also classified acetaldehyde that's produced from drinking alcohol as Group 1. (Acetaldehyde in general, from all sources, has a separate, lower classification as a possible human carcinogen.) The cancers most clearly linked to alcohol include cancers of the mouth, throat, voice box, esophagus, liver, colon and rectum, and female breast.

Acetaldehyde is thought to drive much of this risk because it damages DNA directly and interferes with the cell's ability to repair DNA. It's not the only way alcohol raises cancer risk, but it's one of the most important.

A few points worth knowing:

- **Acetaldehyde is made in your mouth, too.** Bacteria in your mouth and saliva can turn alcohol into acetaldehyde locally. That's one reason the mouth, throat, and esophagus are especially exposed.
- **Smoking compounds it.** Tobacco smoke contains acetaldehyde of its own. Drinking and smoking together raise the risk of mouth and throat cancers far more than either alone.
- **The risk tracks with amount.** The more you drink over the years, the higher the risk. Health agencies including the US Surgeon General have stressed that there's no level of drinking that's completely free of cancer risk, though the added risk from light drinking is small.

None of this means one night out gives you cancer. It does mean the long-term pattern of drinking matters, and that people who flush have an extra reason to keep it light.

## Where Else Is Acetaldehyde Found?

Alcohol metabolism is the biggest source for most drinkers, but acetaldehyde shows up in other places too:

- **Alcoholic drinks themselves.** Fermentation produces some acetaldehyde directly. Levels vary by drink and how it was made, and some spirits and fortified wines tend to contain more.
- **Tobacco smoke**, as mentioned above.
- **Foods.** Small amounts occur naturally in ripe fruit, coffee, bread, and fermented foods such as yogurt, vinegar, and kombucha. It's part of what gives some of these foods their flavor.
- **Industry.** Acetaldehyde is used to make other chemicals, plastics, and resins, and it's present in vehicle exhaust and some indoor air.
- **Your own body.** Gut bacteria and normal metabolism produce tiny amounts even if you never drink.

For a social drinker, the amounts from food are small compared with what alcohol produces in the body. The two exposures you can meaningfully control are how much you drink and whether you smoke.

## Medicines That Can Raise Acetaldehyde

Some medicines interfere with the ALDH enzyme or are linked to reactions that look like acetaldehyde build-up. If you take any of these, follow your label and talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking.

- **Disulfiram (Antabuse).** This drug blocks ALDH on purpose. Drinking while taking it causes flushing, pounding heart, nausea, vomiting, and in some cases a dangerous drop in blood pressure. The reaction can happen for days after the last dose.
- **Metronidazole and tinidazole.** These antibiotic and antiparasitic drugs carry warnings against alcohol because of reports of disulfiram-like reactions. Researchers have debated how strong the effect really is, but the label advice is still to avoid alcohol during treatment and for a few days afterward.
- **Some other medicines.** Certain older antibiotics, some diabetes pills, and a few other drugs have been linked to similar reactions. Ask your pharmacist if you're unsure about yours.

A disulfiram-type reaction can be serious. If you take one of these medicines and feel faint, have chest pain, or have trouble breathing after drinking, get emergency care.

## How to Lower Your Acetaldehyde Exposure

There's no shortcut that makes your liver clear acetaldehyde dramatically faster. The approaches that actually work are simple:

1. **Drink less.** Less alcohol in means less acetaldehyde made. This is the only approach that reliably lowers both short-term symptoms and long-term risk.
2. **Drink slower.** Spacing drinks out, ideally to about one an hour, gives ALDH2 a chance to keep up instead of letting acetaldehyde pile up.
3. **Eat before and while drinking.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your liver, which smooths out the peak.
4. **Don't smoke while drinking.** It adds acetaldehyde from a second source and multiplies cancer risk.
5. **Take flushing seriously.** If you flush, that's your body telling you acetaldehyde is high. Drink less or skip it rather than masking the redness with antihistamines.
6. **Look after your mouth.** Some research suggests good oral hygiene reduces the bacteria that make acetaldehyde from alcohol in saliva. It's a small factor, but it costs nothing.

For more on what does and doesn't change how quickly your body processes alcohol, see our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism). Spoiler: very little works beyond time.

## Supplements and Products That Claim to Target Acetaldehyde

Because acetaldehyde is a well-known villain, many hangover products market themselves around it. Here's an honest look at the main categories.

### ZBiotics

ZBiotics is a probiotic drink made with bacteria that have been genetically engineered to produce an acetaldehyde-breaking enzyme. The idea is that the bacteria break down some acetaldehyde in your gut. The concept is plausible, but most acetaldehyde is made and cleared in the liver, not the gut, and independent human research on hangover outcomes is limited. Some people swear by it; others notice nothing. We compare it in detail in our [DHM vs ZBiotics](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-zbiotics) article and our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review).

### NAC (N-acetylcysteine)

NAC is a building block for glutathione, the body's main antioxidant, which helps protect cells from reactive molecules, including acetaldehyde. Some animal research suggests cysteine-type compounds can bind acetaldehyde, and a small older human study of L-cysteine reported reduced hangover symptoms in some participants. The evidence is early and mixed. Our [NAC vs DHM comparison](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025) covers this in more depth.

### DHM (dihydromyricetin)

DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Mouse studies, including work from researchers at the University of Southern California published in 2020, have suggested DHM may increase the activity of alcohol-processing enzymes and lower acetaldehyde levels in animals, as well as support liver health. Other research suggests it acts on GABA receptors in the brain, which may explain why some people report feeling clearer the next day. The key caveat: most of this evidence comes from animal and lab studies, and human data are still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents the alcohol flush reaction in people with the ALDH2 variant, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe or reduce alcohol's long-term cancer risk.

Our [DHM science explainer](/never-hungover/dhm-science-explained) walks through what the studies do and don't show.

### What to be skeptical of

Be wary of any product claiming to "eliminate" acetaldehyde, "neutralize" alcohol's toxins, or make drinking risk-free. Nothing on the market changes the basic fact that your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, and no supplement cancels out the cancer risk tied to drinking.

## When to See a Doctor

Most mild flushing or a slightly worse hangover is not an emergency. But some signs deserve attention.

**Talk to a doctor if:**

- You've started flushing, getting hives, or feeling unwell after small amounts of alcohol when you didn't before. Rarely, new alcohol intolerance can be a sign of another condition or a medicine interaction.
- You flush strongly and drink regularly anyway. Your doctor can talk with you about your cancer risk, and in some places screening may be worth discussing.
- You're unsure whether one of your medicines interacts with alcohol.

**Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if:**

- You have trouble breathing, a tight throat, or swelling of the face, lips, or tongue after drinking. That can be a serious allergic-type reaction.
- You have chest pain, fainting, or a very fast or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle.
- You've taken disulfiram or another medicine with an alcohol warning and react strongly after drinking.
- Someone can't be woken, is confused, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and the person shouldn't be left to "sleep it off."

## The Bottom Line

Acetaldehyde is the toxic middle step in how your body breaks down alcohol. Your liver makes it with the ADH enzyme and clears it with the ALDH2 enzyme, usually quickly enough that levels stay low. When it builds up, you get flushing, a racing heart, nausea, and headache. It likely contributes to hangovers, though inflammation, poor sleep, and other factors matter too. Its biggest long-term importance is cancer: acetaldehyde from drinking is classified as a cause of cancer in humans, and people who flush face a higher risk if they drink regularly.

The reliable ways to limit it are to drink less, drink slower, eat first, avoid smoking, and treat flushing as a signal rather than something to hide. If you want to explore supplements as an extra on top of those habits, keep your expectations modest. DHM has interesting early research, mostly in animals. If you'd like to try it, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly single-ingredient pick, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [best DHM supplements](/never-hungover/best-dhm-supplements) roundup compares the main brands. For broader habits that make the biggest difference, start with our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is acetaldehyde in simple terms?**

Acetaldehyde is the chemical your liver makes when it starts breaking down alcohol. It sits between alcohol and acetate, a harmless end product, and it's much more toxic than alcohol itself. Most people clear it quickly with an enzyme called ALDH2, but when it builds up it causes flushing, a racing heart, nausea, and headache.

**Does acetaldehyde cause hangovers?**

It likely contributes, but it isn't the whole story. Hangovers usually peak when blood alcohol is near zero, and by then acetaldehyde levels in most people are also low. Researchers now think hangovers come from several things together, including the immune system's inflammatory response, poor sleep, dehydration, congeners in darker drinks, and acetaldehyde.

**How long does acetaldehyde stay in your body?**

In people with a normal ALDH2 enzyme, acetaldehyde is cleared about as fast as it's made, so it doesn't linger once the alcohol is gone. Your body processes roughly one standard drink per hour, so acetaldehyde production continues for as long as alcohol remains in your blood. People with the ALDH2 variant behind Asian flush clear it much more slowly and reach higher levels.

**Why does acetaldehyde make your face turn red?**

Acetaldehyde widens small blood vessels in the skin and is linked to the release of histamine, the same chemical involved in allergic reactions. That causes redness and warmth in the face, neck, and chest. People with a slow version of the ALDH2 enzyme build up more acetaldehyde, which is why they flush after small amounts of alcohol.

**Is acetaldehyde a carcinogen?**

Yes. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies acetaldehyde produced from drinking alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen, meaning it causes cancer in humans. It damages DNA and interferes with DNA repair. It's linked especially to cancers of the mouth, throat, and esophagus, and the risk rises with how much you drink over time and is higher if you also smoke.

**How can I get rid of acetaldehyde faster?**

There's no reliable way to make your liver clear it dramatically faster. What works is making less of it in the first place: drink less, drink slower, eat before and while drinking, and don't smoke while drinking. Some supplements are marketed for acetaldehyde, but the human evidence for them is limited.

**Does DHM lower acetaldehyde?**

Some animal studies suggest DHM may boost the activity of alcohol-processing enzymes and lower acetaldehyde levels, but human data are still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents the flush reaction in people with the ALDH2 variant, and it doesn't reduce alcohol's long-term cancer risk. Treat it as a possible extra on top of drinking less and slower, not a substitute.

**Does taking Pepcid before drinking stop acetaldehyde?**

No. Antihistamine-type heartburn pills like famotidine (Pepcid) can reduce the visible redness of Asian flush, but they don't lower acetaldehyde at all. Researchers have warned that hiding the flush can lead people to drink more while their tissues are still exposed to high acetaldehyde levels.
